statement_record.book: Given F : X → Y and G : Y → Z, their composite is the function X → Z sending x to G(F(x)) — evaluate F at x, then evaluate G. Usually written G ∘ F, but the book prefers the diagrammatic order F ; G, writing the first-applied function on the left.

statement_record.book: A preorder relation on a set X is a binary relation, written infix ≤, such that (a) x ≤ x for all x and (b) x ≤ y and y ≤ z imply x ≤ z. NO antisymmetry is required. When both x ≤ y and y ≤ x hold one writes x ≅ y and calls x and y equivalent. A preorder is a pair (X, ≤).
statement_record.intree: `Program Definition Proset {A : Type} {R : relation A} (P : PreOrder R) : Category := {| obj := A; hom := R; … id := reflexivity…; compose := …transitivity… |}` and `Record TwoPreorder := { tpre_carrier : Type; tpre_le : …; tpre_refl x : tpre_le x x; tpre_trans x y z : tpre_le y z → tpre_le x y → tpre_le x z; tpre_dec … }`, with `Program Instance hom_preorder {C : Category} : PreOrder (@hom C)` for the converse reading.
statement_record.strength_comparison: same. Proset consumes exactly the two axioms — stdlib `PreOrder R` is Reflexive + Transitive and nothing else — and the hom-type IS R, so the book's relation and the library's arrows coincide; identity is reflexivity and composition transitivity, and the header states explicitly that antisymmetry is not required, so distinct objects may be isomorphic. TwoPreorder is the book's pair (X, ≤) as a record with the two laws as fields; note the same-name-but-weaker trap in that direction — it carries an EXTRA field `tpre_dec x y : tpre_le x y + (tpre_le x y → False)`, decidability, needed only so the enrichment can compute an object of 2, so it is a decidable preorder rather than the general notion (the general notion is Proset over stdlib PreOrder). The book's `x ≅ y` for mutually related elements is the library's ordinary isomorphism (Theory/Isomorphism.v), which in a Proset amounts to R x y together with R y x because both iso laws are equations in the trivial hom-setoid `equiv := fun _ _ => True`; that unfolding is nowhere stated as a lemma, though Test/Poset.v:102 and :150 state precisely the mutually-related hypothesis pair `(x ~> y) → (y ~> x) → x = y` for the two poset examples. Instance/Props.v is an in-tree preorder that is genuinely not a poset (logically equivalent but distinct propositions), witnessing the definition's point that ≅ is weaker than =.

statement_record.book: Reflexivity and transitivity are exactly two of the three axioms of an equivalence relation (Definition 1.18), so a preorder is precisely an equivalence relation with the symmetry axiom dropped.
statement_record.intree: `Program Instance hom_preorder {C : Category} : PreOrder (@hom C) := { PreOrder_Reflexive := fun _ => id; PreOrder_Transitive := fun _ _ _ f g => g ∘ f }` on one side, `Class Setoid A := { equiv : crelation A; setoid_equiv : Equivalence equiv }` on the other, with `Proset (P : PreOrder R) : Category` realizing the two-axiom notion.
statement_record.strength_comparison: intree-weaker: both endpoints are in-tree in exactly the axiom shapes the remark compares, and over a SHARED vocabulary (both `PreOrder` and `Equivalence` come from Coq.Classes.RelationClasses and are built from the same `Reflexive` / `Symmetric` / `Transitive` classes, so the containment the remark points out is visible in the imported vocabulary), but no in-tree statement draws the comparison. statement_record.book: Every set X carries the discrete preorder in which the order relation is equality: the only instances of x ≤ y are x ≤ x, and for distinct x, y neither x ≤ y nor y ≤ x holds. Depicted as a collection of unconnected points.
statement_record.intree: `Program Definition DiscreteCat (A : Type) : Category := {| obj := A; hom := fun x y => x = y; … id := fun _ => eq_refl; compose := fun _ _ _ g f => eq_trans f g |}` with `Lemma DiscreteCat_Discrete (A : Type) : Discrete (DiscreteCat A)` over `Discrete C := ∀ x y (f : x ~> y), ∃ H : x = y, f ≈ rew H in id`.
statement_record.strength_comparison: same. The order relation is propositional equality itself — `hom := fun x y => x = y` is the book's '≤ is =' verbatim — with reflexivity as eq_refl and transitivity as eq_trans, so the resulting thin category is the discrete preorder; DiscreteCat_Discrete asserts the second half of the item contrapositively: any arrow forces x = y, hence for distinct x, y neither direction is inhabited. Lemma DiscreteCat_Discrete@{o h p} (A : Type@{o}) : Discrete (DiscreteCat@{o h p} A).  — over `Discrete C := ∀ x y (f : x ~> y), ∃ H : x = y, f ≈ rew H in id`, hence a fortiori: in a discrete preorder mutually related elements are equal, i.e. it is already a partial order

statement_record.book: A partial order (poset) is a preorder satisfying the additional axiom that x equivalent to y implies x = y; in categorical language this axiom is skeletality, so partial orders are exactly the skeletal preorders. The distinction is inessential: every preorder becomes a partial order by identifying (quotienting by) equivalent elements. Every discrete preorder is already a partial order, whereas a codiscrete preorder collapses to the unique partial order on a one-element set.
statement_record.intree: `Definition Poset {C : Type} `{R : relation C} `(P : PreOrder C R) `{@Antisymmetric C eq eq_equiv R} : Category := Proset P`; `Lemma poset_nat_skeletal : forall x y : obj[Poset_nat], (x ~> y) -> (y ~> x) -> x = y` (and poset_two_skeletal); `Lemma DiscreteCat_Discrete (A : Type) : Discrete (DiscreteCat A)`.
statement_record.strength_comparison: intree-weaker. The definitional half is faithful and the categorical reading is even stated in prose: Instance/Poset.v defines a poset as exactly a Proset plus `Antisymmetric` and its header records that 'antisymmetry adds nothing to the underlying Category construction … it only makes the resulting thin category skeletal, so that isomorphic objects are equal', citing nLab's 'a poset is exactly a skeletal thin category'. The skeletality condition is ASSERTED only per instance, as poset_nat_skeletal and poset_two_skeletal, in the book's own form (mutually related objects are equal). The first illustration is in-tree (DiscreteCat_Discrete gives that a discrete preorder is already skeletal); the second is not, since the codiscrete preorder does not exist in-tree at all (see 7sketches:1.2.2:example33). The remark's substantive claim — that the distinction is inessential because every preorder quotients to a poset — has no in-tree counterpart.

gap: Two precise pieces. (1) Skeletality is not a notion in the library: there is no `Skeletal` predicate or lemma of the form `∀ x y, x ≅ y → x = y` stated for an arbitrary category (grep -rn --include='*.v' -i 'skeletal' → Test/Poset.v's two per-instance lemmas plus prose in Instance/Poset.v:19-21, Instance/Two.v:86-88 and Theory/Equivalence.v:92-98; Structure/Discrete.v's `Discrete` is discreteness, strictly stronger, not skeletality), so 'partial orders are exactly the skeletal preorders' cannot be stated in-tree, only per example. (2) The posetal reflection is absent: nothing quotients a preorder by mutual relatedness to produce a poset — grep -i 'skeleton' → only prose, and Theory/Equivalence.v:92-98 explicitly records that the library 'confines skeletons to concrete instances'; grep -iE 'posetal reflection|poset reflection|quotient of a preorder|identify equivalent' → 0 hits. Construction/Quotient.v quotients a category by a hom-congruence (identifying parallel ARROWS), which cannot identify OBJECTS and so is not the construction required.

statement_record.book: A graph is a quadruple (V, A, s, t): a set V of vertices, a set A of arrows and functions s, t : A → V; an arrow a with s(a) = v, t(a) = w is an arrow from v to w. A path is a finite sequence of arrows in which the target of each is the source of the next — explicitly including paths of length 1 (a single arrow) and of length 0, which begin and end at the same vertex and traverse no arrow.

The book's quadruple becomes `nodes` plus `edges : nodes → nodes → Type` with the edges INDEXED by their endpoints, so source and target are implicit in the indexing; the file header states the translation outright ('In the classical presentation this is two sets V, E with source/target maps s, t : E → V; here the edges are indexed directly by their endpoints … Parallel edges and loops are allowed'), and Instance/Parallel.v:166 exhibits the quadruple form itself, as a presheaf on the walking parallel pair with source := fst and target := snd.
